review: The Arabic addresses the Lord in the singular throughout (نَرْفَعُ … أَسْتَرِيح … أَشْتَهِي), and stanza 3 quotes Song 1:4 (اجْذِبْنِي فَنَجْرِي وَرَاك); the Hebrew keeps the same movement from 'we' in stanza 1 to 'I' in stanza 3, because the hymn is the soul speaking inside the congregation.

2:1–2:4 נִרְדִּי וְהֵרִיחַ … רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ — Song 1:12 (נִרְדִּי נָתַן רֵיחוֹ) with the sacrificial רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ (Gen 8:21); the Arabic نَارِدِينِي قَدْ أَفَاح / رَائِحَةً زَكِيَّةً is that nard, and the Hebrew keeps the Song's own noun.

3:1–3:2 מָשְׁכֵנִי … וְנָרוּץ אַחֲרֶיךָ — Song 1:4 exactly (מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָרוּצָה); the Arabic is that verse, and the singular 'draw me' with plural 'let us run' is kept rather than smoothed out.

4:1 אַהֲבָתְךָ תִּלְחָצֵנִי — the Arabic فَحُبُّكَ يَحْصُرُنِي is 'Your love constrains me'; לָחַץ is the biblical verb for pressing/hemming in (Ps 42:10), so the line keeps the pressure of 2 Cor 5:14 rather than the Modern Hebrew מְחַיֵּב.

1:3–1:4 אֵין יָדִיד זוּלָתְךָ / בּוֹ לְעוֹלָם אֶשְׁקֹט — the Arabic فَلَا حَبِيبَ غَيْرَكَ / بِهِ دَوَامًا أَسْتَرِيح is 'no beloved but You, in whom I ever rest'; יָדִיד is the noun of Deut 33:12 and Isa 5:1, and the Hebrew attaches the rest to Him rather than to the beloved in general.
